title: Origins of Vampire Mythology

jokes.text: Best friends making a cake. Wait. Ah. Best friends making a cake. Pow.
jokes.setup: Abed is apparently narrating or describing his own actions while doing something domestic, treating a mundane activity with cinematic gravitas.
jokes.punchline: 'Pow.' — the deadpan escalation of the narration to a sound effect lands as pure Abed, treating cake-making like a superhero origin story.
jokes.explanation: The joke works entirely because of character integration — Abed treating a mundane act as a cinematic moment is his entire comedic identity. 'Pow' as the punctuation is perfectly economical. Not a classic but a strong opener that establishes the episode's emotional underpinning (Abed wants a best friend).

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Bye bye bye!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Don't want to hear you say goodbye!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: We're gonna miss you!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: So much!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: When we're gone!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You'll cry!

jokes.text: How come I'm not best friends with anyone? Aww. Don't patronize me.
jokes.setup: Abed makes a genuinely sad, self-aware observation about his social situation.
jokes.punchline: The group responds with 'Aww,' and Abed immediately snaps back 'Don't patronize me' — refusing comfort while still having invited it.
jokes.explanation: Classic Abed move — emotional vulnerability immediately undercut by his own deflection. The rhythm is sharp: vulnerability, sympathy, rejection of sympathy. Very economical and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You know, sometimes I wonder if any of you actually like me, or if you just feel obligated because we study together.

dialogue.speaker: Group
dialogue.line: Aww, Pierce...

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Oh, shut up! I don't want your pity. That's worse than not liking me.

jokes.text: She'll be coming around the mount dean when she comes. Whoo-whoo!
jokes.setup: The Dean arrives to make an announcement, apparently entering dramatically.
jokes.punchline: He riffs on 'She'll be coming 'round the mountain' replacing it with 'mount dean' — a narcissistic pun delivered with full theatrical commitment and a train sound effect.
jokes.explanation: The pun itself is middling but the Dean's total commitment to his own wordplay — and the 'whoo-whoo' train sound — elevates it. Very Dean-specific in its combination of narcissism and corniness.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Random personal declaration about trains

jokes.text: I have an ex-boyfriend that travels with a carnival.
jokes.setup: Someone asks if the carnival company is called Red Beard's Amusements.
jokes.punchline: Britta reveals she has a carnival ex-boyfriend — the absurdity of this being her personal connection is the joke, delivered flatly.
jokes.explanation: Classic Britta self-reveal — the comedic premise that Britta has terrible taste in men is well-established, and a carnival worker ex fits perfectly. The flat delivery is the joke. Good setup for the episode's main comic thread.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: Choo choo! All aboard!

jokes.text: Some things are funny because they make no sense. That's not one of them.
jokes.setup: Someone (likely Jeff) makes a dismissive comment about Britta's carnival ex being funny.
jokes.punchline: Abed provides analytical commentary on the nature of comedy itself, then applies it critically to the current situation.
jokes.explanation: Very Abed — he's doing comedy criticism in real-time while being part of the scene. The meta quality works because it's also genuinely insightful. 'That's not one of them' as the kicker is economically perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: His name is... Subway.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Like the sandwich place?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Oh no.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Britta, what were you thinking?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's worse than any of her other decisions.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I dated a girl named Olive once. Different situation.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Lord have mercy.

jokes.text: Well, it looks like my news has incited some doings. And if that's not my job, what is? Choo-choo!
jokes.setup: The Dean's announcement about the carnival has caused a reaction among the study group.
jokes.punchline: The Dean takes credit for 'inciting doings' as his core job function, then caps it with another train sound — escalating the new train obsession gag.
jokes.explanation: The 'choo-choo' callback lands because we now know the Dean is 'into trains.' 'Incited some doings' is a funny euphemism for chaos. The Dean's self-satisfied incompetence is well-played.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: She's right. We're laughing at her pain, which is the same thing that's happening to us right now — we're laughing at a character laughing at a character's pain. It's meta-comedy, which means the joke is on us, which means we should feel bad, which means we're laughing at ourselves feeling bad. It's a perfect loop.

jokes.text: So, Britta, tell us about your carnival-worker boyfriend. So you all can get a laugh? Yeah. I'd love to. The exact reason. Fine, I'm not ashamed of my past. And if it entertains you, great, because we're friends.
jokes.setup: Jeff bluntly asks Britta to share embarrassing personal information for the group's entertainment.
jokes.punchline: Britta tries to call him out, but then agrees anyway — reframing it as friendship rather than humiliation — which is funnier than refusing would be.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's brazen honesty ('The exact reason') is a good character beat, and Britta's capitulation while maintaining dignity is true to both characters. Functional exchange that moves the scene forward while getting laughs.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, your name is Blade? Like the Marvel character?

dialogue.speaker: Blade
dialogue.line: Yes, that's my name.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm gonna need you to stop that immediately. Marvel's lawyers are very aggressive.

jokes.text: His name is Blade. / She invoked friendship to undercut the laugh, and we're still laughing. That's how funny it is.
jokes.setup: Britta reveals her ex-boyfriend is named Blade, then pre-emptively deploys their friendship to soften the mockery.
jokes.punchline: Jeff acknowledges Britta's gambit and points out it failed — the name is so funny it overrides even social guilt.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's meta-commentary on comedy mechanics within the scene ('she invoked friendship to undercut the laugh') is sharp writing. It's funny AND it's about being funny, which is very Community. The double reveal — the name AND Jeff's analysis of Britta's failed maneuver — earns a high score.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You're such a nerd for knowing all that comic book stuff.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Oh yeah? Well you knew Britta's boyfriend's favorite beer without her telling you. That's pretty nerdy too.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's different.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Is it though?

jokes.text: His name is Blade. Is that legal? Shouldn't New Line Cinema be suing? He was called that before that stupid movie. He was called that before the fantastic movie?
jokes.setup: The name 'Blade' triggers a pop culture argument.
jokes.punchline: Jeff corrects 'stupid movie' to 'fantastic movie,' defending the Blade franchise while simultaneously mocking Britta.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's correction of Britta's film assessment ('the fantastic movie') while also dunking on her ex is efficient multi-layered comedy. The suing joke is functional. Good ensemble rapid-fire beat.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Britta's taste in men is so bad, she dated a guy who thought a turn signal was a suggestion.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Then she dated someone who microwaved fish at work.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: And finally, a guy who dog-eared his books. She's basically dating characters from a Dostoevsky novel at this point.

jokes.text: It was a Marvel comic in 1973. Well, nerd alert. Well, ex-boyfriend named Blade alert.
jokes.setup: Britta defends the name Blade's pre-movie origins; Jeff calls her a nerd.
jokes.punchline: Britta retorts with her own 'alert' — reframing her knowledge as less embarrassing than her actual situation (having dated someone named Blade).
jokes.explanation: The parallel structure ('nerd alert' / 'ex-boyfriend named Blade alert') is clean and sharp. Britta wins this exchange comedically by owning her embarrassment more thoroughly than Jeff anticipated. The escalation of her own self-roast is very well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, what does that mean?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: It means you put your... look, never mind. You're not ready for this conversation.

jokes.text: Her love life makes Pierce seem with it. Her pain unifies us. She has the King Arthur of bad taste in men.
jokes.setup: The group piles on commentary about Britta's romantic history.
jokes.punchline: Three separate observations escalate in absurdity: Pierce comparison, Abed's clinical observation about pain as social glue, then 'King Arthur of bad taste.'
jokes.explanation: 'King Arthur of bad taste in men' is a genuinely good line — the incongruity of noble legend applied to romantic catastrophe is funny. Abed's 'her pain unifies us' is characteristically clinical and funny. Pierce-as-baseline-for-'with it' is a reliable character joke.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I was just trying to make a joke. Why does everyone always assume the worst about me?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I know I'm not always... politically correct. But I'm not a bad guy. I just say things without thinking sometimes.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: And now nobody wants to hang out with me because of it. Which, I guess, is fair. But it still sucks.

jokes.text: I need to be reminded that he is the worst man on earth. If he comes through town and calls me, I will be there in five minutes.
jokes.setup: Britta declares she needs to be reminded Blade is terrible.
jokes.punchline: Immediately undercuts it by admitting she'd drop everything to be with him in five minutes.
jokes.explanation: Classic self-aware-but-powerless comedy. Britta's self-contradiction is the core of the episode's emotional premise, and the 'five minutes' specificity makes it funnier. Very good character work — only Britta could deliver this exact contradiction.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Blade? What kind of name is Blade? It's so stupid. Although, to be fair, the first two movies were actually pretty good.

jokes.text: Andre much? Okay, I understand. I don't. You will. What's that mean? He's hung.
jokes.setup: Shirley makes a knowing reference to her own husband André to explain Britta's situation. Jeff doesn't understand. Pierce cuts to the most vulgar possible explanation.
jokes.punchline: 'He's hung.' — Pierce's blunt sexual explanation delivered just as Jeff was being led to understand it delicately.
jokes.explanation: Two words, maximum impact. Pierce cutting through Shirley's delicate setup with the bluntest possible answer is both character-specific and structurally satisfying. The escalating mystery ('you will understand') makes the flat punchline more explosive. The joke itself isn't original but the execution is clean.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I love having a locker. Do you know how many outfit changes I can do in a day now?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I've already done three. I'm on my fourth. By lunch, I'll have cycled through my entire wardrobe twice.

jokes.text: No, God. Pierce, you're disgusting. Just like that I'm disgusting again. I was one of the gang. It was in my hand.
jokes.setup: Pierce's vulgar remark gets him called disgusting.
jokes.punchline: 'I was one of the gang. It was in my hand.' — Pierce's pathetic lament that group acceptance was so fleeting, expressed in a way that's even more inadvertently suggestive.
jokes.explanation: 'It was in my hand' — the accidental double entendre following a conversation about sexual endowment is perfect. Pierce's genuine pathos about being briefly accepted makes it funnier. The joke works on two levels and is very character-specific to Pierce's outsider status.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So what do you guys think? Does this work?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Not at all.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I didn't even finish the outfit.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Doesn't matter.

jokes.text: So, what Britta? You're in love with a guy who's named after a kickboxing vampire movie? A fantastic kickboxing vampire movie.
jokes.setup: Jeff summarizes Britta's predicament dismissively.
jokes.punchline: He corrects himself mid-sentence to insist Blade is a 'fantastic' kickboxing vampire movie — he can't help defending it even while making a point.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's compulsive need to defend the Blade franchise — interrupting his own speech — is a great running character beat. The self-correction is perfectly timed and reveals something true about Jeff (he has pop culture pride even at the worst moments). Second callback to 'fantastic.'

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Troy! That is completely inappropriate!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: What? It's a classic movie reference. I'm just saying, like in When Harry Met Sally, we could—

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I don't care what they did in the movie! You can't just say things like that!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Why not? Harry and Sally figured it out. Maybe we should just—

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, stop talking!

jokes.text: No, I don't believe in love because of this guy named after a kickboxing vampire movie. Oh, Britta. / Oh, sweetie. / Oh, Britta.
jokes.setup: Britta clarifies she doesn't love Blade — she just can't resist him.
jokes.punchline: The group responds with simultaneous 'Oh, Britta' / 'Oh, sweetie' — treating the distinction as meaningless, which is more damning than disagreement.
jokes.explanation: The group's synchronized pity is funnier than any rebuttal. 'Oh, Britta' as a phrase is essentially a complete thought — it means 'you are your own worst enemy' — and the group deploying it in chorus is a strong ensemble beat.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I have a weakness for Blade. You know, the vampire hunter? Wesley Snipes? I just... I can't help myself. He's so dangerous and mysterious.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So what you're saying is... he really knows how to... fill in your blank squares?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That's not funny.

jokes.text: You wanna watch Blade tonight? Yes.
jokes.setup: The group has just thoroughly mocked Britta for her attraction to someone named after the Blade franchise.
jokes.punchline: Jeff and Britta immediately agree to watch the Blade movie together, undercutting the entire lecture.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the scene. Four words resolve all the tension by revealing Jeff and Britta are equally hypocritical. 'Yes.' from Britta is instant — no hesitation. The economy is excellent. It earns its laugh through logical inevitability.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Annie, I need help with my addiction comparison essay. Like, what's something you're addicted to?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Um, I don't know. Studying?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Okay, so you're addicted to studying like I'm addicted to... what if we're both addicted to the same thing but in different ways?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: That doesn't make sense, Britta.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: What if I'm addicted to thinking about being addicted to thinking about addiction, and you're addicted to thinking I'm not thinking about it?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I'm leaving.

jokes.text: Oh. I love that I have a locker now. All that wasted time going to my car for mid-afternoon wardrobe adjustments.
jokes.setup: Jeff is at his locker, apparently thrilled to have one.
jokes.punchline: The reason is revealed: he makes 'mid-afternoon wardrobe adjustments' — implying he keeps multiple outfits in his car, which he now keeps in a locker. It's a window into Jeff's ludicrous vanity.
jokes.explanation: Deeply character-specific — only Jeff would (a) make mid-afternoon wardrobe changes, (b) do so from his car, and (c) treat a school locker as a luxury upgrade. The specificity of 'mid-afternoon' is key. This is the kind of small joke that expands the character world richly.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Britta's really into that guy. She's like, desperately into him. I've never seen her like this before.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You know what? I think I know how she feels. Women get like that around me sometimes. It's just something I have to deal with.

jokes.text: What do you think? Hm? Stick with what's working? You're gonna change? Not if it's working. It's not working. Yeah. You're right. I knew it.
jokes.setup: Jeff asks Annie for fashion validation, clearly fishing for a compliment.
jokes.punchline: Annie honestly tells him it's not working, and Jeff deflates immediately — his confidence entirely dependent on external validation.
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — Jeff's narcissism punctured by Annie's honesty. 'I knew it' is a nice touch, suggesting he feared this all along. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: All aboard! Next stop, administration! Choo choo! *adjusts conductor hat* The 4:15 to—

dialogue.speaker: Visitor
dialogue.line: Excuse me, where's the registrar?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Sir, if you could just wait until I've completed my—

dialogue.speaker: Visitor
dialogue.line: I'm in a hurry.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: But I haven't even gotten to the part where I mime the coupling mechanism!

jokes.text: I'll have what she's having. Hey, grow up, lady.
jokes.setup: Jeff apparently makes a 'When Harry Met Sally' reference in some context.
jokes.punchline: Annie's response 'Hey, grow up, lady' is a subversion — she's calling out the reference as immature rather than playing along.
jokes.explanation: The joke is a bit context-dependent (unclear what exactly triggers the WHMS reference), but Annie's dismissal is sharp. The 'lady' in Annie's retort is a funny incongruity — she's young, telling an older man to grow up. Moderate.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Troy is a very talented student of the African-American persuasion.

jokes.text: I need to stay with you this weekend. Not just stay with you, I need to be on lockdown. You were a pillhead, so think of Blade as Adderall. Handcuff me to the radiator like a mother-flipping carny-banging werewolf.
jokes.setup: Britta asks Annie for help resisting Blade, escalating her requests.
jokes.punchline: 'Handcuff me to the radiator like a mother-flipping carny-banging werewolf.' — the simile is so specific and unhinged it functions as pure comedic escalation.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The Adderall comparison is clever (using Annie's past to contextualize Britta's addiction), but 'mother-flipping carny-banging werewolf' is a genuine comedic invention — combining profanity censorship, carnival worker specificity, and supernatural imagery into a single perfect simile. Highly quotable, deeply Britta. This earns its 8+ because no other character could say this, and the specificity is extraordinary.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I need your help with something, but I can't be specific about what it is.

dialogue.speaker: Secretary
dialogue.line: Um, okay? What do you need help with?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I just told you, I can't be specific. But it's urgent and it might involve... alcohol.

dialogue.speaker: Secretary
dialogue.line: Dean, I really need more information.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Fine. I'm completely helpless and I have no idea what I'm doing with my life.

jokes.text: I got this. Our apartment has central heating, but I get the idea, stay strong.
jokes.setup: Britta asks to be handcuffed to the radiator.
jokes.punchline: Annie notes there's no radiator (central heating) but agrees to the spirit of the request — treating the logistical correction as the most important thing to address.
jokes.explanation: Annie's earnest pedantry — correcting the radiator detail mid-emotional-crisis — is very Annie. The deadpan pivot from practicality to emotional support is perfectly timed.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Blade has these silver stakes, and he uses them to—

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Can we please not talk about Blade right now?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: But Blade's the best vampire hunter! He's got—

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I think she means her ex, Blade.

jokes.text: I wonder how many women I've affected this way.
jokes.setup: Jeff has been listening to Britta's crisis about not being able to resist Blade.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's takeaway is narcissistic self-reflection — wondering how many women HE has made similarly desperate.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Jeff Winger joke. As Britta describes her inability to resist a charming man, Jeff's mind goes to himself. The line is delivered as genuine introspective curiosity, not bragging — which makes it both funnier and more damning. Very high character integration: this joke could ONLY be Jeff. Economy is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Can I ask you something? And I want you to answer honestly.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: If you were texting with someone, would you tell me?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Because if you were, and you didn't tell me, and I found out from someone else, I don't know if I could ever trust you again. I mean, we'd probably have to move to separate countries. Change our names. I'd become a interpretive dancer in Montreal.

jokes.text: Whoo, whoo! All aboard the human being railway.
jokes.setup: The Dean arrives/walks past, now fully committed to his train persona.
jokes.punchline: 'All aboard the human being railway' — he's given the train obsession a name and a philosophy.
jokes.explanation: Third iteration of the train gag — 'human being railway' is a good new addition (applying the metaphor to his administrative role) but the joke is running on fumes from the stronger earlier iterations.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I'm not saying I need my phone, I'm saying that in today's society, constant connectivity is essential for personal safety and professional obligations. It's about being responsible.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You're addicted to your phone.

jokes.text: Oh, a wonderful opportunity for a young man of urban race.
jokes.setup: The Air Conditioning Repair School head is pitching Troy's enrollment to the Dean.
jokes.punchline: The Dean's response is a cringe-worthy racial euphemism — 'urban race' — that is meant to be awkward rather than clever, exposing the Dean's oblivious cluelessness.
jokes.explanation: Classic Dean cringe — the joke is his oblivious racism/euphemism, not actual racism. The show deploys this carefully. 'Urban race' is meant to be awkward in-world. Functions as characterization comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Oh my god, what is this?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We need to talk to you about something.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: We've all been very concerned.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: This is an intervention.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: We even wrote it down so you wouldn't feel blindsided.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: There's a message on the banana.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: We love you, and that's why we're doing this.

jokes.text: Mine is not to tell you how to do what I want done. Mine is to want and to say my want. Yours is to know and to do.
jokes.setup: The mysterious AC Repair School figure is explaining the power dynamic to the Dean.
jokes.punchline: The elaborate pseudo-poetic breakdown of their respective roles ('mine is to want and to say my want') is so pompously absurd it becomes funny.
jokes.explanation: The AC Repair School's grandiose self-importance is a running joke across the season — this instance of making bureaucratic hierarchy sound like feudal mythology is a good manifestation. The repetitive structure ('mine... yours') makes it sound like a villain's monologue delivered about paperwork.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Why won't you unblock me?! I'm not even mad, I'm just frustrated!

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: You know what? Fine. You're being really immature about this.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Actually, you're being downright stupid. Like, genuinely dumb.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: You're a sentient turd! A walking pile of incompetence!

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: You're basically Batman, but if Batman was made of wet spaghetti and bad decisions!

jokes.text: Natalie, could you get me a, um, book on how to do things?
jokes.setup: The AC head has just told the Dean 'yours is to know and to do' — implying he should figure out how to get Troy into the program.
jokes.punchline: The Dean's response is to ask his secretary for 'a book on how to do things' — the most generic possible interpretation of being told to act.
jokes.explanation: One of the best Dean jokes in the episode. After being told grandiosely to 'know and to do,' his response is to ask for a self-help book with the most uselessly vague title imaginable. 'A book on how to do things' is perfectly economical absurdist comedy — it's the most helpless possible interpretation of authority. High character integration, high economy. Earns its 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: She just called me the opposite of Batman.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: What's the opposite of Batman?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I have no idea. But I'm pretty sure I'm not it.

jokes.text: You know, just make a Scotch and soda. Make it yourself. I don't know how.
jokes.setup: The Dean tells his secretary to 'just make a Scotch and soda' as an alternative to the book.
jokes.punchline: She refuses; he admits he doesn't know how to make a Scotch and soda — the man who was just told to 'know and do' cannot even make a simple cocktail.
jokes.explanation: Good extension of the previous joke — the Dean's incompetence made concrete. 'I don't know how' as a confession about cocktail-making while he's supposed to be strategizing is excellent bathos. Quick and effective.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Pierce, if you ever tell anyone about the things we do together, I will destroy you.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: What things? We don't do anything.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Exactly. And I'd like to keep it that way.

jokes.text: I love Blade's special weapons. Yeah. See that sword? It has two blades. One is silver, the other is infused with garlic.
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed are watching Blade while Britta tries to resist calling her ex.
jokes.punchline: Troy and Abed's earnest film analysis — appreciating a movie sword's dual vampire-killing properties — is funny because of their total absorption in the film, oblivious to Britta's crisis.
jokes.explanation: Functional background comedy — Troy and Abed's innocent enthusiasm for the movie is charming but not exceptional. Sets up the Blade-discussion-as-trigger joke that follows.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I found a best friend.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Chang? Really? That's like saying you found the best gas station on the highway. Sure, it exists, but nobody's aspiring to that.

jokes.text: I should check my messages. No. / What word? 'Blade.' / Because of Britta's ex. Can you check my messages?
jokes.setup: Britta is on lockdown. Troy innocently says 'Blade' in the context of the movie.
jokes.punchline: Even the word 'Blade' is enough to trigger Britta's craving — and her immediate pivot to phone-checking is transparent. Troy's innocent 'What word? Blade?' makes it worse.
jokes.explanation: Good sustained cringe — Britta's addiction-like response to the word 'Blade' parallels the Pavlovian trigger of her phone anxiety. Troy's oblivious repetition of the word is a small escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: So what do you want to do today?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I don't know, maybe we could play some Russian roulette?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa. That's a little intense, don't you think?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: What? You're the one who suggested it!

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: No I didn't! I said we could play... uh... Parcheesi. Parcheesi roulette.

jokes.text: Annie, think for one second. You have my phone. You're not even checking it. What if my mother is dying? You just wanna know where your phone's hidden. I just wanna know if my mother is dying. It's a simple yes or no. I'll cover my eyes. You go check and say, 'No, your mother isn't dying,' or 'Yes, your mother is dying,' and then we go back to watching the film.
jokes.setup: Britta claims she just wants to know if her mother is dying as a pretext for getting her phone back.
jokes.punchline: Britta's elaborate 'simple yes or no' negotiation plan — 'I'll cover my eyes, you go check' — reveals the transparent desperation of an addict bargaining, culminating in her calmly saying 'and then we go back to watching the film.'
jokes.explanation: The escalating negotiation is very well-structured — Britta's 'simple' plan becomes more elaborate with each sentence, revealing her desperation. 'And then we go back to watching the film' is the perfect deadpan button, treating a potential maternal death as a brief administrative inconvenience. Strong Britta character work.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Blade is way better looking than Jeff.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Shirley, come on.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: What? I'm not just saying that because you're here. Blade is genuinely more attractive.

jokes.text: Give it to me. That's right, Britta. It's a banana.
jokes.setup: Britta is reaching desperately for her hidden phone.
jokes.punchline: Annie has hidden a banana in its place — Britta reaches for her phone and gets a banana instead.
jokes.explanation: Classic physical setup with a great reveal — the banana swap is both a practical joke and a dramatic visual. 'That's right, Britta. It's a banana.' delivered as though it's a profound revelation is excellent. The banana is also a visual gag when it appears on screen. Very well-executed surprise.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Blade is an aspirational figure for the African-American community. He's a hero who doesn't apologize for his sexuality or his desire for vengeance. He's a man who understands that sometimes you have to embrace your darkness to save yourself.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: C'est magnifique, non?

jokes.text: I'm sure those words hurt. But you wouldn't be reading them if they weren't true.
jokes.setup: Britta has presumably read something written on the banana.
jokes.punchline: Annie has pre-written a message on the banana — the idea that she planned this in advance, wrote words on a banana, and deployed it strategically is funnier than the content.
jokes.explanation: Annie pre-writing an intervention message on a banana — delivered with total sincerity — is deeply character-specific. Only Annie would (a) think of this, (b) execute it this way, and (c) treat the banana inscription as a solemn message. The earnestness of 'I'm sure those words hurt' is pitch-perfect.

jokes.text: I am so weak. But we are not defined by our limitations. We are defined by our potentials. I have the potential to watch Blade.
jokes.setup: Britta reads an inspirational message off the banana and applies it to her situation.
jokes.punchline: She transforms the inspirational message into justification for watching the movie — 'I have the potential to watch Blade.'
jokes.explanation: Perfectly structured subversion — the inspirational language ('defined by our potentials') is set up sincerely then immediately torpedoed by applying it to watching a vampire movie. 'I have the potential to watch Blade' is a legitimately great line. The logic is internally consistent, which makes it funnier. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: You're my sister now.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: What? No, I'm not!

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Yes, you are. Sisters share everything. Now give me your phone.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: That's not how this works!

jokes.text: You two are bad friends. Bad. / That's unfair. What about you guys? You don't like our movie, we can't say 'Blade', there's phones in the refrigerator. Oops.
jokes.setup: Britta calls Troy and Abed bad friends for not helping her.
jokes.punchline: Troy accidentally reveals the phone is in the refrigerator by listing it as an example — his defense inadvertently giving away the secret.
jokes.explanation: Structurally elegant — Troy's self-defense accidentally reveals the information that defeats the entire scheme. The 'oops' is perfectly placed. This is a classic comedy-of-errors beat executed with real craft. The setup (Britta listing grievances) is a vehicle for Troy's slip, and it lands cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I switched our phones so you'd have to listen to me.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: That's like if Blade had a gun that made you not a vampire anymore. That's not a gift, that's a curse!

jokes.text: Let me see if he called. I have a right to know. You're monsters. You're Hitlers! You're racist pedophiles! You're the opposites of Batman! You don't know what that means. Gonna rip out your throats and eat your...
jokes.setup: Britta is trying to get to the refrigerator where her phone is hidden.
jokes.punchline: Her insults escalate from 'monsters' to 'Hitlers' to 'racist pedophiles' to 'the opposites of Batman' — an escalation that gets progressively more absurd until it circles back to childish.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout moments. The escalation from 'monsters' → 'Hitlers' (plural!) → 'racist pedophiles' → 'the opposites of Batman' follows perfect comedic escalation logic while also being subverted — 'the opposites of Batman' is so abstract that Abed/Troy rightly point out she doesn't know what that means. The interruption mid-throat-ripping is also funny. Highly quotable, deeply Britta. 'The opposites of Batman' alone is a classic.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Britta, your passive-aggressive behavior is unacceptable, and frankly, your psychology degree is a joke. Also, it's 'narcissism,' not 'narcissim.' You spelled it wrong on your business cards.

jokes.text: Still think the lock was overkill? No.
jokes.setup: Britta has just gone into full meltdown mode trying to get to her phone.
jokes.punchline: Annie asks if the extreme measures (locking Britta in) were overkill; Troy sees the evidence and immediately concedes.
jokes.explanation: Efficient button on the chaos scene. 'No.' as a one-word concession is perfectly economical. Functions as a grace note rather than a standalone joke.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So your name is just... Blade?

dialogue.speaker: Blade
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Like the vampire hunter?

dialogue.speaker: Blade
dialogue.line: I don't know what you mean.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Your parents named you Blade?

dialogue.speaker: Blade
dialogue.line: Mustard is a window into the soul.

jokes.text: 'There's phones in the refrigerator.' / It's you.
jokes.setup: Britta now knows the phone is in the refrigerator.
jokes.punchline: She stands in front of the refrigerator, reads the number calling, and realizes Annie has secretly substituted her own number for Blade's — a dramatic revelation played as a beat.
jokes.explanation: Good scene-closing revelation. 'It's you.' works as both a comedic button and sets up the phone-swap subplot. The dramatic irony (audience might have guessed but Britta hasn't) makes it satisfying.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm not cool anymore. I've lost my edge.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Jeff, you're still cool. You're like the coolest guy here.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: No, Shirley. Blade said—

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Honey, you don't need Blade to tell you you're cool. You just are.

jokes.text: Boys' night. I need help reacting to something. Hi.
jokes.setup: Jeff apparently arrives at Troy and Abed's apartment for 'boys' night.'
jokes.punchline: Jeff's framing ('I need help reacting to something') treats his emotional processing as a masculine collaborative task — he needs backup for having feelings.
jokes.explanation: Jeff needing 'help reacting' is very character-specific — he's incapable of processing emotion alone and frames it as a collaborative project. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Chang, you're my best friend, my brother from another mother.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Pierce, you complete me.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce & Chang
dialogue.line: 🎵 We are friends, forever friends, riding on a rainbow's end! 🎵

dialogue.speaker: Pierce & Chang
dialogue.line: 🎵 Through the highs and through the lows, that's the way our friendship goes! 🎵

jokes.text: Remember, it's just a quick peek at Blade. You tell anyone, I will stop letting you do things with me I'm afraid to tell anyone about.
jokes.setup: Jeff is apparently going to look at Blade (Britta's ex) at the carnival, and needs Troy's complicity.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's threat — 'I will stop letting you do things with me I'm afraid to tell anyone about' — implies he and Troy have a secret activities partnership, suggesting Jeff enjoys Troy's company more than he'd publicly admit.
jokes.explanation: Smart joke that works on two levels: Jeff's vanity (he cares what people think), and the implication that Jeff and Troy have a clandestine friendship with shared activities neither would admit to. The circumlocution ('things I'm afraid to tell anyone about') is very Jeff.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Oh my god, Britta's been texting me all day. Let me read you these...

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: "Hey, remember that thing we talked about?" Okay...

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: "I've been thinking about it a lot." Thinking about what?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: "We need to talk." Oh no...

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: "It's about us." There is no us, Britta!

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: "I can't keep this secret anymore." What secret?!

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: And then... "He has your eyes."

jokes.text: You wanna look at Britta's ex. If you did it by yourself, you'd be weird. You're the only one that understands.
jokes.setup: Jeff has given an elaborate justification for going to the carnival.
jokes.punchline: Troy cuts through it immediately with the simple truth — Jeff wants to scope out Britta's ex and needed company to avoid being weird.
jokes.explanation: Troy's gift for cutting through social pretense with simple honesty is well-deployed here. 'If you did it by yourself, you'd be weird' is both pragmatic and accurate. 'You're the only one that understands' — Troy accepting Jeff's secret compliment with zero fanfare — is a good button.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Dean Pelton, what are you doing here?

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: What am I doing here? I work here, Troy. I'm the Dean.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Oh right, sorry Dean.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: It's okay. It just... it hurts a little.

jokes.text: Oh, funky. Ha! What, are you guys on a date? Pretty awkward. Look what Pierce won me.
jokes.setup: Jeff and Troy encounter Shirley at the carnival with Chang as her companion.
jokes.punchline: Shirley and Chang turn up together at the carnival — the incongruous pairing, with Shirley having 'gone outside the group' for a best friend.
jokes.explanation: The Pierce/Chang pairing at the carnival mirrors Abed's desire for a best friend subplot. The 'on a date' comment from Jeff is a mild joke. Structural comedy — the visual of this pairing — is funnier than any single line.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Some people call me Blade. Some people call me daywalker. I don't really care what you call me.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I just know that vampires are afraid of me, and I'm not afraid of them.

jokes.text: I decided to go outside the group for a best friend. Couldn't do better than Chang? Take that back. He could do plenty better than me. I was the first to say yes.
jokes.setup: Pierce has gone outside the friend group to find a best friend.
jokes.punchline: Chang's self-deprecating admission that Pierce 'could do plenty better than me' — followed by the pathetic 'I was the first to say yes' — is simultaneously self-aware and sad.
jokes.explanation: 'I was the first to say yes' is an excellent joke. Chang acknowledges he's a poor choice for best friend while taking pride in his speed of acceptance — the joke being that his only qualification is desperation. Deeply character-specific to Chang's status as group outcast. High economy, high character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: She's experiencing a mixture of rejection and relief, with a subtle undercurrent of arousal from the leather.

jokes.text: Have fun forcing life. We will. What next? Cotton candy? Russian roulette? What did you say? Cotton candy sounds great.
jokes.setup: Jeff dismisses Pierce and Chang's forced friendship.
jokes.punchline: Chang suggests 'Russian roulette' as a logical next activity after cotton candy — delivered deadpan — then immediately pivots to cotton candy sounding great when Pierce seemingly doesn't register it.
jokes.explanation: Chang's 'Russian roulette' as a casual carnival activity suggestion is a great dark comedy beat — it hints at his unhinged nature while being played completely straight. Pierce apparently mishearing makes it better. The recovery ('cotton candy sounds great') is perfectly timed.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Look, I'm not saying these relationships are real, but they're not NOT real. They exist in a space between reality and... Dean-ality.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Besides, I may have altered some transcripts to make sure my imaginary girlfriend meets the prerequisite requirements for advanced courses. It's called love, people.

jokes.text: What next? Cotton candy? Russian roulette? / What did you say? Cotton candy sounds great.
jokes.setup: Pierce suggests their next activity together.
jokes.punchline: He casually includes 'Russian roulette' between carnival activities, then Chang's innocent redirect ('cotton candy sounds great') implies he may have heard the Russian roulette suggestion and chosen to let it pass.
jokes.explanation: Good dark beat — Pierce's casual inclusion of Russian roulette in an activity list implies a certain darkness in his view of a fun afternoon. Chang's pivot to cotton candy is played completely straight, which is funnier than acknowledgment would be.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I didn't cheat on that law school exam. I used magic.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Magic? Chang, that's impossible.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: And that's why a magician never reveals his secrets.

jokes.text: He's not as good-looking as you. / I wasn't fishing for that. / No. I offered it freely.
jokes.setup: Shirley and Jeff are observing Blade at the carnival.
jokes.punchline: Shirley proactively compliments Jeff's looks compared to Blade — she 'offers it freely' without being asked, suggesting she knows Jeff well enough to know he needs it.
jokes.explanation: 'I offered it freely' is a great line — Shirley being proactively complimentary because she knows Jeff's ego needs it, while Jeff's denial ('I wasn't fishing') is transparently false. Good character dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm not studying Blade because he's black. I'm studying Blade because he's a master of multiple fighting disciplines, he has impeccable fashion sense, and he's a daywalker. Those are universal themes that transcend race.

jokes.text: I want to go on a ride. This is a window for me. I spent my carnival years pregnant.
jokes.setup: Shirley expresses a desire to go on a carnival ride.
jokes.punchline: 'I spent my carnival years pregnant.' — a brief, devastating biographical reveal explaining why she missed out on carnival rides.
jokes.explanation: Five words of dark backstory delivered with perfect economy. 'My carnival years pregnant' implies this was a recurring pattern, not a one-off event. Very Shirley — mixing cheerful surface with dark biographical reality. The specificity ('carnival years' as a distinct life phase) makes it funnier and sadder simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: So how do we make sure we don't end up fighting like this?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: We just need to be honest with each other. No secrets, no passive-aggressive comments.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You're right. Like when you borrowed my stapler and never gave it back?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I gave it back! And it's not even a big deal!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Not a big deal? It had my name on it!

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Oh, so NOW we're talking about the stapler? This is exactly what I was worried about!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Well maybe if you hadn't brought up 'no secrets,' I wouldn't have mentioned it!

jokes.text: I'm not jealous. I just wanted to see what the deal was. Obviously the deal is he's a dirtball, Britta hates herself, voilà.
jokes.setup: Jeff is watching Blade and processing his own reaction.
jokes.punchline: Jeff diagnoses the entire situation with false certainty ('voilà') while clearly still being bothered — 'voilà' as an attempt to close the case on something he's still obsessing over.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's self-delusion is well-deployed here — the 'voilà' is trying too hard to seem casual. Character-specific but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Blade, come on. I spent good money on this. You have to tell me your secret.

dialogue.speaker: Blade
dialogue.line: I don't owe you anything, Winger.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Please. Please. I'm begging you. Just tell me. What is it? How do you do it?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I need to know. I NEED to know!

jokes.text: I want you to know and I've never said these words, but I've always felt them: You're a sister to me.
jokes.setup: Britta begins what sounds like a sincere, heartfelt declaration of friendship to Annie.
jokes.punchline: The build-up ('I've never said these words, but I've always felt them') creates expectation for something profound — it lands as 'you're a sister to me,' which is genuine but also sets up Britta immediately trying to manipulate Annie.
jokes.explanation: The setup works as emotional misdirection — the moment feels real, then immediately becomes a manipulation tactic. The rewatch value is high because knowing Britta is about to use this against Annie makes the declaration both funny and a little sad.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I've been thinking about this moment for weeks.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Really? Because it seems like you've been thinking about it for about five seconds.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Well, yes, but those were very intense seconds.

jokes.text: I have to call my doctor for some results. Don't worry, I'm fine. It's just a little personal. You need privacy, sure thing. I'll check on you later.
jokes.setup: Annie has just handed over the phone in a 'gateway of trust.'
jokes.punchline: Britta immediately deploys a vague medical excuse to get privacy so she can call Blade — Annie, being Annie, immediately respects her privacy without question.
jokes.explanation: Functional comedy of manners — Britta's manipulation and Annie's naivety. Well-played but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You switched the phone numbers on us?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Well, you switched them first!

jokes.text: You came out smiling, then your smile faded as you leaned against the door. I gave Britta her phone. You did? Why? She needs to feel trust to recover.
jokes.setup: Troy has apparently observed Annie's body language precisely.
jokes.punchline: Troy's exact narration of Annie's physical reactions — delivered as normal conversation — is funny because of its precision and suggests Troy pays extremely close attention to people.
jokes.explanation: Troy's hyper-observant narration is a mild character joke. Functional but not a highlight.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Blade is brain damaged.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Jeff, that's a terrible thing to say!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: No, I mean literally. He has brain damage. Look at the medical report.

jokes.text: No. I secretly switched Blade's number in her phone to my number. She tries to get in touch, it'll come to me.
jokes.setup: Troy suggests Annie has made a mistake by giving Britta her phone.
jokes.punchline: Annie reveals she executed a sophisticated phone-number switch — the reveal that sweet, earnest Annie has been running a covert operation.
jokes.explanation: The reveal of Annie's secret operation is good character comedy — she's not as naive as she appears, and her competence at manipulation is funnier because of her earnest surface. Sets up the entire phone-swap subplot.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, so Blade's got this mysterious confidence, right? Turns out when he was seven, he got his head stuck in a funnel cake machine at the county fair. They had to shut down the whole ride to get him out. He was in there for like forty minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: When they finally got him out, the doctors said he had some swelling, but he'd be fine. Except... he wasn't fine. He came out of that funnel cake machine with this weird, unshakeable confidence. Like the machine had rewired his brain to believe he was invincible.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So that's why Blade does crazy stuff and never doubts himself. Carnival funnel cake machine brain damage. It's actually beautiful in a way.

jokes.text: She's probably just telling him she's 'dying to feel the warmth of his...' Are you kidding me? She said we were sisters. I'm so sad right now.
jokes.setup: Annie hopes Britta is staying strong; Troy has no such illusions.
jokes.punchline: Troy's knowing prediction of Britta's sexting — his reading of the situation being immediately confirmed ('Are you kidding me?') — reveals Annie's betrayal more completely than a direct statement would.
jokes.explanation: Troy's accurate prediction and Annie's dawning horror work as a good double-beat. 'She said we were sisters' as Annie's main wound is funny — the manipulation was what stings, not the relapse.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Look, Britta, relationships are like a class you're taking. You show up, you do the work, and sometimes you realize you're not actually enrolled and you've been sitting in the wrong room for three weeks.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That's... actually kind of wise?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I know, right? I'm basically a therapist. That'll be $200 an hour.

jokes.text: And she is so co-dependent. And such a bad speller.
jokes.setup: Troy is reading Britta's texts to Blade (really to Annie's number).
jokes.punchline: Troy's clinical diagnosis of co-dependence followed by the mundane observation that she's a bad speller — the two criticisms given equal weight.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest lines. The structure is perfect: a serious psychological observation ('co-dependent') immediately equated with a petty practical one ('bad speller'). The bathos of treating both as equally damning criticisms is excellent comedy. Troy's matter-of-fact delivery is essential. Very quotable. Earns its 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You know what I've noticed about apartment buildings? They're designed by people who have never actually lived in them. Like, why is the thermostat always in the worst possible location?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Mine's right next to the front door, so every time someone leaves, the temperature drops twenty degrees and the system kicks in. I'm basically paying to air-condition the hallway.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: And the walls are so thin, I can hear my neighbor's conversations. Last week I learned their entire relationship history without ever meeting them. They should really consider that as a tenant screening tool.

jokes.text: A nom de corn dog? Why would I have a carnival name? Your parents named you Blade? Apparently. Well, you seem okay with it. Not much to do about it. You could change it. To what? Templeton Ferrari III? Won't change how mustard tastes.
jokes.setup: Jeff probes Blade about his unusual name, expecting him to be defensive.
jokes.punchline: Blade's total equanimity ('not much to do about it') followed by 'Templeton Ferrari III? Won't change how mustard tastes.' — a philosophical non-sequitur that defies follow-up.
jokes.explanation: The best line in the episode. 'Templeton Ferrari III? Won't change how mustard tastes.' is extraordinary comedy writing. It does multiple things simultaneously: (1) the specific absurdity of 'Templeton Ferrari III' as the alternative name, (2) the zen philosophy of the mustard metaphor — suggesting identity is in the experience, not the label — (3) it explains Blade's entire character (no shame, no ego, total acceptance) in one line, and (4) it makes Jeff and the audience completely understand why women can't shake this guy. Nom de corn dog is also a great inciting line. This approaches the craft of the anchor '8.0' example and arguably exceeds it in originality.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I've been thinking about building quirks. You know, like how every building has its own personality? This one has character flaws.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Yes! Exactly! It's like the air conditioning—

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: The air conditioning works exactly how it's supposed to, which is never.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: That's what I was gonna say!

jokes.text: Won't change how mustard tastes. I get it. I see the appeal.
jokes.setup: Blade has delivered his 'mustard' philosophy.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's immediate capitulation — 'I get it. I see the appeal.' — after one interaction with Blade, confirming that even Jeff is not immune to his charm.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's near-instantaneous conversion after dismissing Blade all episode is both funny and character-revealing. His admission is unusually honest, suggesting Blade's shamelessness genuinely disarms him. Good callback.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm in my imaginary room right now, completely isolated from the world. Nothing can touch me here.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Wait... is this bathroom... real?

jokes.text: He's relaxed, he's cool. Not as cool as you. / Mr. Blade, I want three more rounds. Jeffrey! Not gonna change the way mustard tastes. Oh, and you're so cool, Shirley. Sometimes I am.
jokes.setup: Jeff is competing at the duck gallery while trying to understand Blade's appeal.
jokes.punchline: Shirley keeps offering Jeff unsolicited reassurance ('not as cool as you'), and Jeff's repeated invocation of the mustard philosophy is now being used as a cool-sounding dodge.
jokes.explanation: Shirley's running 'not as cool/handsome as you' reassurance to Jeff (who clearly needs it) is a good recurring bit. Jeff adopting 'mustard' as a philosophy within seconds of hearing it is a quick self-parody.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You brush your teeth like you're doing physical comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I do!

jokes.text: Mr. Blade, I want three more rounds. / Jeffrey! Not gonna change the way mustard tastes. / Oh, and you're so cool, Shirley. Sometimes I am.
jokes.setup: Jeff is now also falling under Blade's spell, buying more rounds at the booth.
jokes.punchline: Shirley cites the mustard line back at Jeff ('not gonna change the way mustard tastes'), now using it as wisdom. When Jeff mockingly calls her 'so cool,' she accepts it sincerely: 'Sometimes I am.'
jokes.explanation: The mustard line has now become currency in the conversation — Shirley using it against Jeff is a good callback escalation. 'Sometimes I am' as Shirley's response to being called cool is a quietly great line: sincere, surprising, and slightly badass.

jokes.text: How many times are they gonna do that? This is it, isn't it? We're becoming best friends. I think so. I think so.
jokes.setup: Pierce and Chang have apparently been watching Jeff get reassured by Shirley repeatedly.
jokes.punchline: Pierce and Chang have a sincere 'best friends' realization in parallel with Jeff and Shirley's dynamic — their friendship is a parody of the main group's relationships, happening in real-time.
jokes.explanation: Pierce and Chang's sincere parallel to the episode's friendship theme — them deciding to be best friends through pure proximity — is a good structural joke. The double 'I think so' is tender and absurd.

jokes.text: Oh, my God. One after the other. 'I'm texting to tell you I'm not texting you anymore. I'm sorry, I didn't mean that. Are you mad at me now?'
jokes.setup: Annie is reading Britta's texts sent to Annie's number (which Britta thinks is Blade's).
jokes.punchline: The texts reveal a classic anxious attachment pattern — the 'I'm texting to tell you I'm not texting you' self-contradiction is the comedic peak.
jokes.explanation: 'I'm texting to tell you I'm not texting you anymore' is a perfect articulation of anxious attachment self-contradiction — it's funny because it's both absurd and painfully recognizable. The escalating texts reveal a fully realized character portrait in three sentences. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Fine. I guess you don't wanna know our 2-year-old.
jokes.setup: Britta's texts to 'Blade' (really Annie) have been escalating.
jokes.punchline: Britta invents a child — a '2-year-old' — as emotional leverage in the text conversation, escalating from 'are you mad at me' to introducing a fictional baby.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest moments. The escalation from 'are you mad at me' to introducing a '2-year-old' as emotional leverage is both shocking and perfectly in-character for Britta's escalating desperation. 'Our 2-year-old' — the casual possessive pronoun, the specificity of the age — is extraordinary economy. The implication that she's willing to invent a child to keep someone's attention is both dark and very funny. Earns 8.5 craft.

jokes.text: Can we please put it under a stack of mattresses? When is she gonna take a hint?
jokes.setup: Britta's texts are coming in one after another.
jokes.punchline: 'Under a stack of mattresses' — Annie's escalating solution to Britta's texts is to bury the phone physically, treating Blade's attention like a Princess and the Pea problem.
jokes.explanation: Annie's physical escalation (put it under mattresses) mirrors Britta's textual escalation and is a mild absurdist image. Functional.

jokes.text: Britta's attracted to unavailable men. Dean, why are you here? Ouch.
jokes.setup: The Dean has apparently arrived at Annie and Britta's apartment uninvited.
jokes.punchline: 'Dean, why are you here?' followed by 'Ouch.' — the third iteration of the Dean being told he has no reason to be in a scene, which he takes personally every time.
jokes.explanation: Running gag that lands — the Dean's 'Ouch' at being questioned about his presence is funnier each time because his hurt is genuine. Very economical.

jokes.text: Fine. Let's make him available. What are you doing? Ending this. 'Leave me alone.' No! No! That's so much worse. See? She stopped.
jokes.setup: Jeff decides to impersonate Blade via text to make Britta stop texting.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's 'Leave me alone' makes things dramatically worse, then magically works — but his success metric ('See? She stopped') ignores that it only worked because it's crueler.
jokes.explanation: Good beat — the well-intentioned cruelty of Jeff's 'fix' (being mean to Britta 'as Blade') landing as 'that's so much worse' then immediately working. His logic is ironically correct. Annie's horror at the method vs. the result is a good dynamic.

jokes.text: No! No! / That's so much worse. / See? She stopped.
jokes.setup: Dean sends the 'leave me alone' text as Blade.
jokes.punchline: Annie's 'that's so much worse' vs. Dean's 'see? She stopped' — both technically true, neither addressing the other's concern. Dean measures success by the cessation of texts, Annie by the actual state of Britta's psyche.
jokes.explanation: Good competing-definitions-of-success joke. 'She stopped' is a technically accurate but morally hollow victory that Dean claims with pride. The exchange captures something true about institutional vs. personal metrics of success.

jokes.text: She's calling him? She was born in the '80s. She still uses her phone as a phone.
jokes.setup: Britta is now calling rather than texting.
jokes.punchline: Troy's generational observation — that people born in the '80s still use phones for actual phone calls — delivered as a genuine character flaw.
jokes.explanation: 'She still uses her phone as a phone' is an excellent observational joke that also works as generational comedy. Troy's deadpan delivery of phone-calling as a character flaw specific to '80s births is both sharp and very quotable. Economically perfect — two sentences do a lot of work.

jokes.text: Hello? Blade? [silence beat — Annie realizing Britta is calling her number]
jokes.setup: Britta calls Blade's number — which is actually Annie's number.
jokes.punchline: Annie is in the room and her phone rings. The audience and Annie both realize simultaneously that Britta is calling her. The silence/beat before anyone speaks is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the phone-swap plot. The awkward silence when everyone realizes what's happening is the comedic peak — a situation joke that relies entirely on structure and timing. The economy is perfect: 'Hello? Blade?' is all it needs.

jokes.text: There you go. I don't know. Change your settings so it doesn't go to voicemail. Too late.
jokes.setup: Britta's call to 'Blade' has gone to Annie's voicemail.
jokes.punchline: Jeff and Annie scramble to manage the situation — 'Too late.' as the button when the voicemail picks up is clean.
jokes.explanation: Functional plot-mechanism comedy. The 'Too late' button works but doesn't add much. Transitional.

jokes.text: Step right up. Ding, ding, ding! Get your popcorn here. Hello? Busy, babe. Blade, just wait. Wait, Bla... I told you not to call me at work.
jokes.setup: Britta has called Annie's voicemail, then the call is somehow picked up — the group has to impersonate a carnival.
jokes.punchline: Jeff, Troy, Abed, and Annie all impersonate carnival sounds and characters to sell the illusion that 'Blade' is at work. 'I told you not to call me at work' is the perfect exit line.
jokes.explanation: The carnival impersonation sequence is high-energy ensemble comedy — the group has to improvise a full carnival atmosphere, which is both desperate and hilarious. 'I told you not to call me at work' as the capstone line (after all the chaos) delivers a sharp punchline that also advances Britta's character dynamic with Blade.

jokes.text: 'I'm sorry, I forgot. Don't be mad at me.' She's whipped by an imaginary douche.
jokes.setup: Britta responds to fake-Blade's 'don't call me at work' with an apology.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's characterization — 'whipped by an imaginary douche' — is both accurate and funny, with 'imaginary' adding a layer since Blade is now a collective fiction.
jokes.explanation: 'Whipped by an imaginary douche' is a great, economical line that captures the full absurdity of the situation — Britta is being controlled by someone who isn't even present, only a simulation. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Hey, don't knock it till you try it. I got my fake bachelor's degree, and then I cheated on the LSAT. You're wondering how do you cheat on the LSAT? How? A magician never reveals his secrets, my friend.
jokes.setup: Jeff is apparently commenting on being psychologically controlled by an imaginary figure — drawing a parallel to his own history.
jokes.punchline: Jeff reveals he cheated on the LSAT, then refuses to explain how ('a magician never reveals'), treating profound personal fraud as a parlor trick.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's matter-of-fact disclosure of cheating on the LSAT — delivered as life advice — is very character-specific. The 'magician never reveals' deflection is both funny and revealing: Jeff treats his fraudulent past as a performance skill rather than moral failure. High character integration.

jokes.text: So you dropped out of high school and joined the carnival. And 15 years later, here you are. That's about it.
jokes.setup: Jeff is sizing up Blade's life trajectory while competing at the booth.
jokes.punchline: Blade's 'That's about it' — total equanimity about a life narrative that Jeff is clearly framing as a failure — reveals Blade's shamelessness without Blade noticing he's being judged.
jokes.explanation: Blade's equanimity is the joke — 'That's about it' as a complete, satisfied summary of a life Jeff is clearly trying to indict. Good character contrast and Blade's shamelessness is well-illustrated.

jokes.text: What is your end game here? I don't know. I wanna know. What? I wanna know what drove Britta crazy about him.
jokes.setup: Shirley confronts Jeff about his obsession with Blade.
jokes.punchline: Jeff admits he genuinely doesn't know his end game — a rare honest confession — then pivots to wanting to understand Blade's power over Britta.
jokes.explanation: Transitional character beat — Jeff's honest confusion is a good vulnerability moment, but it's more character drama than comedy.

jokes.text: Are you jealous? Are you in love with Britta? No, I am not in love with Britta. Yes, I'm jealous of him. What's his secret? Why do you wanna know the secret to making a woman psycho?
jokes.setup: Shirley presses Jeff on his motives.
jokes.punchline: Jeff distinguishes between being jealous OF Blade (wanting his confidence) vs. being in love with Britta — a subtle distinction that reveals something real about his insecurity.
jokes.explanation: Shirley's 'secret to making a woman psycho' reframe is a good line. Jeff's admission ('Yes, I'm jealous of him') is unusually direct. Mostly character drama with comedic elements.

jokes.text: Why do we wanna know how to blow up the earth or grow a human ear on a mouse? In case we have to, Shirley. In case we have to.
jokes.setup: Shirley asks why Jeff wants to know what makes women obsess over men.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's parallel to blowing up the earth and growing human ears on mice — knowledge for its own sake, 'in case we have to' — is an absurdist escalation that Jeff delivers with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. The parallel structure ('how to blow up the earth OR grow a human ear on a mouse') establishes two absurdist reference points, and 'in case we have to, Shirley. In case we have to.' delivers a perfect double punchline with the repetition adding gravitas to the absurdity. It's also genuinely insightful about masculine psychology — knowledge as contingency planning. Earns 8.5+ — this is the kind of line that Community is famous for.

jokes.text: I'm going to find Pierce. Good. One of those bears is mine.
jokes.setup: Shirley decides to leave Jeff to his obsession.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's 'Good' as genuine dismissal, then 'One of those bears is mine' — Jeff is emotionally invested in a carnival prize.
jokes.explanation: Mild callback — Jeff's investment in the carnival prize reveals his competitive nature. Functional.

jokes.text: So this is best friendship. Something else, isn't it? How do we keep it going? How do we know we won't get into a fight? I say we just let it happen. Don't tell me what to do. What's your problem? What's yours? I'm out of here.
jokes.setup: Pierce and Chang are savoring their new best friendship.
jokes.punchline: Within approximately 10 seconds of declaring best friendship, they get into a fight and Pierce leaves — perfectly illustrating the absurdity of trying to 'force life.'
jokes.explanation: Structurally perfect payoff for the Pierce/Chang subplot. The irony of 'how do we know we won't get into a fight?' followed IMMEDIATELY by a fight is excellent. The escalation from tender moment to 'I'm out of here' in under 30 seconds is both funny and a thematic commentary on forced relationships. The 'Don't tell me what to do' trigger is perfect in its pettiness. Very well-constructed. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: We can stop worrying about voicemail now. Back to the matter at hand. What are you doing? Dean, why are you here? Yikes.
jokes.setup: The Dean reappears.
jokes.punchline: 'Dean, why are you here? Yikes.' — fourth iteration of the running gag, but now 'Yikes' replaces 'Ouch' — a slight variation suggesting the Dean is getting progressively more wounded each time.
jokes.explanation: Fourth iteration of the running gag. 'Yikes' vs. 'Ouch' is a small but good variation. The gag is well-calibrated — still funny but appropriately diminishing.

jokes.text: I figured it out. I know exactly what to do. I'm just gonna be really, really, really mean to her.
jokes.setup: The Dean claims to have figured out how to get Troy into the AC Repair program.
jokes.punchline: His plan is simply to be 'really, really, really mean to her' — a strategy that makes no sense in context and reveals the Dean has no plan at all.
jokes.explanation: The Dean's plan being both wrong and incoherent is consistent character comedy. The triple repetition of 'really' mimics someone convincing themselves. Good but not exceptional.

jokes.text: What don't you get about the concept? Britta likes guys who are mean to her. She doesn't like herself. Give me the phone.
jokes.setup: The Dean doesn't understand the plan Jeff apparently suggested.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's confident psychological assessment ('she doesn't like herself') as the basis for his text strategy — delivered as clinical fact — is funny because Jeff is diagnosing others while exhibiting the same behavior.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's armchair psychology works here as both plot mechanism and character irony (he has his own self-esteem issues). Functional.

jokes.text: Hi. What's up? You guys still watching movies? / Hi, dean. Why are you here? Hi, Britta, and ouch.
jokes.setup: Britta calls to check in; the Dean is still there.
jokes.punchline: Britta greets the Dean and asks why he's there. 'Hi, Britta, and ouch' — the Dean now pre-bundles the greeting with his wound at being questioned.
jokes.explanation: Best iteration of the running gag — 'Hi, Britta, and ouch' is an elegant evolution where the Dean now anticipates the slight and pre-absorbs it into his greeting. This is how running gags should evolve.

jokes.text: You don't know about carpentry? Nope. Or aquariums, freshwater or saltwater. Do you have a big wiener? Nope.
jokes.setup: Jeff (impersonating Blade to Britta) is apparently running through a list of Blade's qualifications/characteristics.
jokes.punchline: 'Do you have a big wiener? Nope.' — Jeff's interrogation of himself/Blade arrives at the sexual question Pierce raised earlier, and he answers honestly.
jokes.explanation: Good callback to Pierce's earlier speculation and Jeff's self-deprecating honesty when interrogated. The list (carpentry, aquariums, wiener) is a good comedic escalation. 'Nope' as the frank self-assessment is clean.

jokes.text: I don't get it, Blade. What's your secret? Why do I wanna impress you? Are you dumb or smart? Are you a loser or winner? Or are you just a human mirror? Do we all see what we wanna see in you? A magician never reveals, right? Right. Later. Okay.
jokes.setup: Jeff confronts Blade directly, asking about his power over women.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's pseudo-philosophical interrogation ends with Blade mirroring Jeff's own language ('a magician never reveals, right?') back at him — a callback that makes Blade seem deeper and Jeff more frustrated.
jokes.explanation: Structurally elegant — Blade uses Jeff's own phrase ('magician never reveals') back at him, and Jeff is forced to agree. The 'Later. Okay.' button — Blade just leaving while Jeff stands there having received nothing — is a perfect character moment. This scene crystallizes the episode's theme through comedy.

jokes.text: You wanna know my secret? Yes. Yes, I do. [Blade leans in and whispers — no words heard]
jokes.setup: Blade has agreed to reveal his secret to Jeff after Jeff spent $300 at the booth.
jokes.punchline: Blade whispers the secret — the audience never hears it. We only get Jeff's reaction. The secret is withheld, which is the joke.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best structural jokes. The build to 'You wanna know my secret?' is enormous — the entire episode has been about what makes Blade irresistible — and the secret is whispered inaudibly. The audience never learns it, which is both thematically correct (the secret can't be transmitted, only experienced) and a perfect comedic subversion of the promise of revelation. The economy is perfect: nothing is said and everything is communicated. Earns high craft scores for structural boldness.

jokes.text: What are you doing? I wanna know. Okay, I'm sorry. I was texting with Blade, but it's over now. He's a loser.
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed catch Britta texting.
jokes.punchline: Britta's abrupt 'He's a loser' — delivered after the texts to Annie-as-Blade included 'leave me alone' — reveals she's been broken by fake-Blade's cruelty, not real Blade's charm.
jokes.explanation: Good irony — Britta is 'cured' not by reality but by an imaginary version of Blade being rude. The rewatch value is high because knowing the texts were from Jeff makes her conviction ('he's a loser') both funny and sad.

jokes.text: Uh, uh, uh... Troy. You should really join the Air-Conditioning Repair program. No. Well, that didn't work. That's what I get for improvising. Good night.
jokes.setup: The Dean makes one final attempt to recruit Troy.
jokes.punchline: His entire pitch is 'You should really join the Air-Conditioning Repair program.' Troy says no. The Dean concludes 'Well, that didn't work. That's what I get for improvising.'
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Dean Pelton moment. The entire subplot — the AC head's grandiose demands, the book on 'how to do things,' the Scotch and soda — culminates in the Dean's 'improvised' pitch being a single sentence delivered flat. 'That's what I get for improvising' is perfect: it implies he considered alternatives (the book, etc.) and decided to wing it anyway. Very character-specific, great economy, tremendous structural payoff. Earns 8.5+.

jokes.text: Troy. You should really join the Air-Conditioning Repair program. / No. / Well, that didn't work. That's what I get for improvising. Good night.
jokes.setup: Dean makes a half-hearted attempt to recruit Troy to the AC program.
jokes.punchline: 'Well, that didn't work. That's what I get for improvising.' — Dean immediately debrief himself on his failed attempt with the candor of a failed sales pitch, then leaves.
jokes.explanation: One of Dean Pelton's best moments in the episode. 'That's what I get for improvising' is a perfect line — it implies there was supposed to be a plan, that improvisation was a recognized risk, and that this outcome was predictable. The deadpan self-assessment and immediate departure is exactly the right comedic choice. High economy: the entire joke is two sentences.

jokes.text: I don't get it. He's a vampire, but he can walk around during the day? What is wrong with you? Huh?
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed are (re)watching Blade after the drama has resolved.
jokes.punchline: Troy is apparently asking Abed a question about Blade's vampire physiology. Abed responds with 'What is wrong with you?' — the meta reversal where someone who watches Blade can't believe a companion doesn't understand Blade lore.
jokes.explanation: Mild coda joke — the episode began and ended with Blade (the movie) being watched earnestly. Abed's 'What is wrong with you?' in response to basic vampire lore questions is a good character beat.

jokes.text: You weren't texting Blade, you were texting us. I switched Blade's number to mine. You tricked me? You tricked me. You ask for my help, you tell me I'm your sister, I do everything I can to make you hate this turd, and the first nice thing he says, and you're over him? Who hurt you? And why didn't it stick?
jokes.setup: Britta realizes she was texting Annie all along.
jokes.punchline: 'Who hurt you? And why didn't it stick?' — Annie's frustrated outburst reveals her own psychological projecting, while also being a genuinely sharp observation about Britta.
jokes.explanation: 'Who hurt you? And why didn't it stick?' is one of the best lines in the episode. It flips the therapeutic question ('who hurt you?') into a lament that the hurt wasn't sufficient to create lasting psychological damage in Britta. It's dark, funny, and deeply character-specific to both Annie's frustrated care and Britta's resilient self-destruction. Highly quotable. Earns 8.5+.

jokes.text: Uh-oh. No, let her go. Lost cause, man.
jokes.setup: Britta is apparently heading for the door after learning Blade isn't a loser.
jokes.punchline: Abed's clinical 'Lost cause, man' — delivered without judgment or urgency — is the perfect deadpan response to watching someone walk into self-destruction.
jokes.explanation: Abed's equanimity in the face of Britta's relapse is very character-specific. 'Lost cause, man' as a verdict is funny in its certainty and lack of drama. Good button.

jokes.text: Jeff, what are you doing here? I just got back from the carnival. Where I met Blade. Is he okay? How is he? He's brain damaged. Let's not be petty. I'm serious. He showed me the scar.
jokes.setup: Jeff reveals he met Blade.
jokes.punchline: Britta asks 'Is he okay?' with concern; Jeff responds 'He's brain damaged' — which Britta interprets as mockery until Jeff clarifies he's serious.
