jokes.explanation: Good misdirection — 'He's brain damaged' sounds like a Jeff insult until 'I'm serious. He showed me the scar.' The pivot to literal brain damage as Blade's secret is both funny and a surprisingly earned reveal. 'Let's not be petty' from Britta is a good defensive reaction.

jokes.text: Ten years ago, before he even met you, a loose bolt flew off a Ferris wheel and embedded in his skull destroying the part of his brain that feels shame. He's basically irresistible to people for the same reason he can pretty much only work at a carnival.
jokes.setup: Jeff explains Blade's secret — a traumatic brain injury.
jokes.punchline: The injury destroyed the shame center of his brain — making him simultaneously irresistible and unemployable outside a carnival context.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best set pieces. The reveal that Blade's mystique is literally a Ferris wheel head injury that destroyed his capacity for shame is both absurd and thematically resonant — the episode's exploration of shame as social control culminates in this joke. 'The part of his brain that feels shame' is a great comic invention. 'Irresistible to people for the same reason he can only work at a carnival' is a perfect, logical irony. Dark, well-structured, deeply original. Earns 8.7.

jokes.text: He's basically irresistible to people for the same reason he can pretty much only work at a carnival.
jokes.setup: Jeff explains the dual consequence of Blade's shame-free existence.
jokes.punchline: The same quality that makes Blade irresistible (no shame) is the same quality that limits his employment to carnivals. The elegant symmetry is both funny and philosophically satisfying.
jokes.explanation: This is a rare sitcom line that actually contains an insight. The structural elegance — irresistible and unemployable for the same reason — gives the joke weight beyond its laugh value. It also functions as a commentary on what we find attractive and why. High craft score for structure and economy.

jokes.text: Why wouldn't he have told me that? He didn't care if you knew. That is so like him. I have to go to him.
jokes.setup: Britta learns about Blade's brain damage.
jokes.punchline: Britta's immediate reaction is 'That is so like him. I have to go to him.' — the brain damage makes him MORE attractive to her, not less.
jokes.explanation: 'That is so like him' applied to a traumatic brain injury — Britta's pattern of finding romantic validation in catastrophe crystallized perfectly. The logic that discovering his brain damage makes him MORE attractive is very Britta. 'He didn't care if you knew' as Jeff's explanation is a perfect deadpan.

jokes.text: No, woman. None of us have to go to anyone. And the idea we do is a mental illness we contracted from commercials and Sandra Bullock. We can't keep going to each other until we learn to go to ourselves. Stop making our hatred of ourselves someone else's job, and just stop hating ourselves.
jokes.setup: Britta is about to run to Blade.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's speech — 'a mental illness we contracted from commercials and Sandra Bullock' — is simultaneously sincere self-help wisdom and absurdist comedy, with 'Sandra Bullock' being the perfect specific-absurd detail.
jokes.explanation: 'A mental illness we contracted from commercials and Sandra Bullock' is an outstanding specific-absurdist line. The speech is genuinely good advice, delivered by Jeff Winger (who is demonstrably terrible at relationships) — the irony is built in. 'Sandra Bullock' is the perfect cultural specificity. This is Community's signature move: sincere emotion packaged in comedy.

jokes.text: Annie, I want you to take my phone. Do not let me call Chang. I'm locking myself in your room.
jokes.setup: Jeff's speech about not going to others has apparently affected Shirley.
jokes.punchline: Shirley immediately hands her phone to Annie — revealing SHE has a Chang dependency — and locks herself away. The episode's Britta plot is immediately replicated with Shirley and Chang.
jokes.explanation: Structurally perfect callback and escalation — the episode's A plot (Britta/Blade phone lockdown) is exactly replicated with Shirley and Chang. 'Do not let me call Chang' mirrors Britta's initial request beat for beat. The revelation that Shirley has a Chang-attachment is both funny and character-consistent. Earns 8.3 for the structural elegance of the callback and the economy of the reveal.

jokes.text: What are you guys doing out here? Self-actualizing. Well, it's loud. Come watch Blade. Okay.
jokes.setup: Jeff and Britta are standing outside, having just resolved their emotional crises.
jokes.punchline: Troy's pragmatic invitation to 'come watch Blade' — and everyone immediately agreeing — undercuts any emotional resolution with the mundane. 'Self-actualizing' as a description of standing in a hallway is also a mild joke.
jokes.explanation: Good deflating button on the emotional arc. The episode begins and ends with Blade (the movie) — the circular structure is satisfying, and 'come watch Blade / okay' is a pleasingly anticlimactic resolution.

jokes.text: This movie is fantastic.
jokes.setup: The group is watching Blade together as a coda.
jokes.punchline: 'This movie is fantastic.' — Jeff's final verdict on Blade, completing his consistent defense of the film throughout the episode.
jokes.explanation: Perfect four-word button. The episode's final non-tag joke completes the 'fantastic' callback arc — Jeff said it was a fantastic movie in the opening scene and says it again at the end, with more weight now. Five words, full circle.

jokes.text: Ever notice that cold spot in the hallway? Oh, yeah. That thing is freezing. You know what could learn a lesson from that? The air-conditioning unit in my living room.
jokes.setup: Abed and Troy are apparently doing a comedy bit in their apartment.
jokes.punchline: Abed notices a cold hallway spot and suggests the living room AC unit should 'learn a lesson from it' — a mundane domestic complaint framed as profound wisdom.
jokes.explanation: Abed and Troy's apartment comedy material is established as a recurring bit in the show. The cold spot / AC unit observation is very 'Abed' — treating a domestic inconvenience with mock profundity. High character integration.

jokes.text: So yesterday, typical Sunday, hanging out in my Dreamatorium. This ever happen to you? I couldn't remember where I imagined the door. Then I realized I was in an actual bathroom.
jokes.setup: Abed is performing observational comedy material at what appears to be an open mic or in-apartment performance.
jokes.punchline: 'I couldn't remember where I imagined the door. Then I realized I was in an actual bathroom.' — Abed's internal world (the Dreamatorium) blurring with physical reality.
jokes.explanation: Deeply character-specific observational comedy — only Abed has a Dreamatorium, and only Abed would confuse an imaginary door with a real bathroom. The joke works as both Abed characterization and a parody of observational stand-up ('This ever happen to you?'). High character integration because it's referencing a season-specific Abed plot element.

jokes.text: No offense, but this material seems pretty specific to your apartment. I don't think it'll work at an open mic.
jokes.setup: Abed has been performing comedy material about their shared living experience.
jokes.punchline: Troy's honest critique — 'this material seems pretty specific to your apartment' — is both a good joke about niche comedy and a meta-comment on the show itself (which IS very specific to these characters).
jokes.explanation: Meta joke that lands — Troy critiquing the material as too niche is also a self-aware comment on Community's own ultra-specific humor. 'Specific to your apartment' as a comedy critique is a good formulation. Very economical.

jokes.text: Ever notice the difference between me and Troy brushing our teeth? I brush my teeth like this: [demonstrates] Troy brushes his teeth like this: [demonstrates different way] / I do. I do. I brush my teeth just like that.
jokes.setup: Abed continues his apartment-specific observational comedy, now doing impressions of their different tooth-brushing styles.
jokes.punchline: Troy's delighted confirmation — 'I do. I do. I brush my teeth just like that.' — suggests Abed's impression is accurate, making the mundane detail genuinely funny.
jokes.explanation: Visual gag inferred from context — Abed is physically demonstrating different tooth-brushing styles. Troy's enthusiastic self-recognition is the comedic payoff. The joke is essentially a celebration of their shared domestic intimacy, which is both sweet and funny.

jokes.text: You know what I'm gonna talk about next. Toaster oven. It's from his album.
jokes.setup: Abed is continuing his comedy set; Troy predicts the next topic.
jokes.punchline: 'It's from his album.' — Troy treating Abed's apartment comedy as a released album with a known track listing is the final meta-joke of the episode.
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode-closing joke. 'It's from his album' implies Abed has performed this material so many times in their apartment that Troy knows it by heart — treating their domestic life as a comedy album is an extraordinary level of character specificity. The economy is near-perfect (four words). This is the kind of line that becomes a fan-favorite moment. Very high character integration — only Troy and Abed could make this joke land.

tmdb_overview: When a carnival comes to Greendale, Annie goes to great lengths to make sure that Britta doesn't contact her carnival worker ex-boyfriend.
insight: Vampire mythology deep-dive hits 57 jokes in 42 minutes—character comedy sustains mediocre impact scores.
